analysis.one_liner: Eliminates out-of-pocket drug costs for Medicare Part D enrollees above their annual cap.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced February 13, 2019 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The RxCAP Act would end all copays and coinsurance for Medicare prescription drug coverage once an enrollee reaches the annual out-of-pocket threshold, starting in 2020. Today, seniors and people with disabilities who hit that cap still pay a share of every additional prescription. The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare enrollees with very high prescription drug costs — typically people with cancer, organ transplants, or other expensive conditions — would pay nothing for drugs once they hit their annual out-of-pocket cap. The low-income subsidy program would be conformed accordingly.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates all cost-sharing (copays and coinsurance) for Medicare Part D enrollees above the annual out-of-pocket threshold, beginning in plan year 2020.
Makes the change retroactively framed so the Part D low-income subsidy's existing catastrophic-coverage provisions stay intact, conforming the LIS program to the new rule.

analysis.who_pays: Drug plans, their premiums/beneficiaries' premium pools, and the federal government would bear the added costs; insurers would absorb what beneficiaries no longer pay above the cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D plans and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not specify a funding mechanism or how insurers would be reimbursed for absorbing costs currently borne by high-cost enrollees, so premiums or federal spending would rise.

It addresses cost-sharing only above the threshold; it does nothing to cap total out-of-pocket spending before that threshold, so enrollees would still face substantial costs each year before protection begins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one percent of Part D enrollees who hit catastrophic costs — many paying thousands a year even after 'catastrophic' coverage — the benefit is concrete and large. The cost, absorbed by plans and ultimately premiums or the federal budget, is real but diffuse. The bill's scope is narrow: it leaves the whole road to the threshold untouched, so most enrollees would see no change.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and immediately referred to the Senate Finance Committee on February 13, 2019; no hearing, markup, vote, or further action ever followed before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced S. 475 on February 13, 2019 with five Democratic cosponsors from the start.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day — the committee whose chairman, Wyden himself, could have scheduled action.
The bill received no further action of any kind for the remainder of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries above the cap who would have paid nothing more for prescriptions are worse off; the status quo's savings accrue to insurers and plan sponsors who kept collecting coinsurance from high-cost enrollees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers kept collecting from high-cost seniors

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 13, 2019 and referred it to the Finance Committee he chairs; did not schedule a markup or floor action.

for.name: 9 Senate Democrats (cosponsors)
for.role: Senators sponsoring the bill (Bennet, Cardin, Klobuchar, Merkley, Whitehouse among them)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 10 sponsors total.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill with no hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined, and Republicans held both the White House and Senate majority.

industries.note: Plans would absorb the cost of care they currently charge high-cost enrollees above the cap, unless premiums or federal payments made them whole.
Removing patient cost-sharing above the cap removes price sensitivity at the point of purchase, but manufacturers retain their existing prices; the bill itself imposes no new price controls.
